2|
3|`photocraft-web-<version>.zip` (from the GitHub release, or `packaging/web/package.sh`) holds a
4|static site in `photocraft-web-<version>/`:
5|
6|| File | What it is |
7||---|---|
8|| `index.html` | The page. It loads everything through relative URLs. |
9|| `photocraft-web-boot-<hash>.js`, `photocraft-web-boot-<hash>_bg.wasm` | A small module (about 120 KB) that starts the app from its parts, with its wasm-bindgen glue |
10|| `app/photocraft-web-<hash>.part-aa`, `-ab`, … | The app's WebAssembly, gzipped and cut into parts of at most 20 MiB (see [Sizes](#sizes)) |
11|| `app/parts.txt` | The parts, in order |
12|| `app/photocraft-web.js` | The app's wasm-bindgen glue (generated, ES module) |
13|| `_headers`, `.htaccess` | Sample header rules for Netlify/Cloudflare Pages and Apache |
14|| `fonts/` (optional) | Fonts loaded on demand, listed in `fonts/manifest.txt` (see [Fonts](#fonts)) |
15|
16|There is no server-side code. Upload the folder's contents anywhere that serves static files.
17|
18|## Docker
19|
20|> The Docker recipe (`Dockerfile`, `.dockerignore`, `packaging/web/nginx.conf`) is
21|> **community-maintained**: it is not built in CI or used for releases, so it can lag behind the
22|> official web build above. Fixes are welcome.
23|
24|From the repository root (Docker is the only build prerequisite):
25|
26|```sh
27|docker build --load -t photocraft-web:local .
28|docker run -d --name photocraft-web --restart unless-stopped \
29|  -p 8080:8080 photocraft-web:local
30|```
31|
32|Open **http://localhost:8080/**. The multi-stage `Dockerfile` builds the existing Rust/Wasm
33|app with Trunk, including HEIF support, then copies only the static site into NGINX. The
34|runtime runs as the `nginx` user on port **8080**, with a `/healthz` endpoint and Docker
35|health check. It serves precompressed gzip assets, the Wasm MIME type, immutable hashed
36|assets, and an HTML page that revalidates after deployments. No Rust installation, Node.js,
37|database, GPU passthrough, or document volume is needed on the host.
38|
39|The first build downloads Rust dependencies and Trunk's Wasm tools and can take several
40|minutes. Subsequent builds reuse Cargo caches. The builder supports Linux amd64 and arm64;
41|the default Rust version is the stable release CI used when the `Dockerfile` was last updated
42|(CI and releases always use the latest stable), and Trunk is pinned to the release workflow's
43|`TRUNK_VERSION`. `RUST_VERSION`, `TRUNK_VERSION`, and `NGINX_VERSION` can be overridden with
44|`--build-arg`. To stamp the About dialog with the commit and date instead of "dev build", pass
45|`--build-arg PHOTOCRAFT_BUILD_SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD) --build-arg PHOTOCRAFT_BUILD_DATE=$(date -u +%F)`.
46|The web build does not embed the optional `craft-fonts` checkout.
47|
48|The Docker build uses thin LTO and one Cargo build job to reduce peak memory, while keeping
49|the web profile's size optimizations and `wasm-opt -Oz`. Its Wasm size may differ from the
50|release zip figures below; NGINX has no 25 MiB file limit. To use the release zip's fat LTO on
51|a builder with more memory, pass `--build-arg CARGO_PROFILE_WASM_RELEASE_LTO=fat`.
52|`--build-arg CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=4` enables more concurrent compilation on larger builders. A compiler killed with
53|`SIGKILL`/`cannot allocate memory` means the Docker/Podman VM needs more memory or swap.
54|
55|For a public deployment, put an HTTPS reverse proxy or your hosting platform's TLS endpoint
56|in front of container port 8080. With a reverse proxy on the same host, bind only loopback
57|(`-p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080`); with a proxy container, connect both through a Docker network.
58|HTTPS enables WebGPU and browser clipboard APIs. If hosting under `/photocraft/`, redirect
59|`/photocraft` to `/photocraft/` and strip that prefix when proxying to the container. Relative
60|asset URLs then work without rebuilding. For example, in an existing HTTPS NGINX server:
61|
62|```nginx
63|location = /photocraft { return 301 /photocraft/; }
64|location /photocraft/ {
65|    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080/;
66|}
67|```

69|The editor and image processing run on the visitor's device. Open uses the browser file
70|picker; Save and Export download files. Preferences use browser localStorage. There is no
71|server-side document storage, desktop TCP control server, or web autosave/crash recovery;

79|## Sizes
80|
81|Measured on 2026-10-13 (0.8.2, `packaging/web/package.sh`):
82|
83|| File | Size |
84||---|---|
85|| `app/photocraft-web-<hash>.part-aa` (the only part today) | 11,401,527 bytes (10.9 MiB) |
86|| `app/photocraft-web.js` | about 170 KB (26 KB with gzip) |
87|| `photocraft-web-boot-<hash>_bg.wasm` and `.js` | about 120 KB together |
88|
89|The app's WebAssembly is 25,019,043 bytes (23.9 MiB) before gzip.
90|
91|Per-file upload limits: Cloudflare Pages and Workers static assets reject any file over
92|**25 MiB** (26,214,400 bytes), and the app's WebAssembly is at that size. (Releases up to 0.2.0
93|shipped a 25.8 MiB wasm, which Cloudflare rejected; issue #198.) So the site doesn't hold it as
94|one file: packaging gzips it and cuts the result into parts of at most 20 MiB, and the page puts
95|them back together while it downloads them. `packaging/web/package.sh` fails if any file in the
96|site is over 24 MiB, so a release can't ship a file a common host refuses, and the app can grow
97|without reaching that limit (issue #5302). A build straight from Trunk (`trunk build --release`
98|in `apps/photocraft-web`, or the Docker image above) still has the app in one `.wasm`, for hosts
99|without such a cap.
100|
101|The app is built with the `wasm-release` Cargo profile (fat LTO, size-optimized code with the
102|pixel and file-decoding crates kept at speed) plus `wasm-opt -Oz`, and stores the bundled fonts
103|(PhotoCraft's and egui's) and the translation catalogs compressed, unpacked on first use.
104|
105|## Any path works
106|
107|All URLs in `index.html` are relative (`public_url = "./"` in `apps/photocraft-web/Trunk.toml`),
108|so the site works at a domain root (`https://example.com/`), under a prefix
109|(`https://example.com/tools/photocraft/`) and from a CDN bucket. The asset names carry a content
110|hash, so they can be cached forever. `index.html`, `app/photocraft-web.js` and `app/parts.txt` keep
111|their names and need revalidation.
112|
113|## Required server settings
114|
115|- **MIME type:** serve `.wasm` as `application/wasm`. Browsers refuse to stream-compile it under
116|  any other type, and the app then loads slowly or not at all. Serve `.js` as `text/javascript`.
117|  Most hosts already do both. For nginx, check that `mime.types` has `application/wasm wasm;`.
118|- **The parts as they are:** serve `app/*.part-*` byte for byte, with no `Content-Encoding` (they
119|  are gzip already, and the page inflates them). Their extension is one servers don't
120|  know, so the usual result, `application/octet-stream` and no compression, is right.
121|- **Missing files are 404s:** a host that answers every unknown path with `index.html` (a
122|  single-page-app fallback) hides a failed upload. PhotoCraft notices and says the download
123|  failed, but a 404 is clearer in the server's logs.
124|- **Compression:** turn on gzip or Brotli for `.wasm`, `.js` and `.html`. It matters little for
125|  the download, since the parts are compressed already; it shrinks the two `.js` files and the
126|  small boot module. You can also precompress and let the server send `Content-Encoding: br`.
127|- **Caching:** `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` on the files whose names
128|  carry a hash (the parts and `photocraft-web-boot-<hash>.*`), and `no-cache` on `index.html`,
129|  `app/photocraft-web.js` and `app/parts.txt`. The sample `_headers` and `.htaccess` do this.
130|- **HTTPS:** WebGPU (and the clipboard) only work in a secure context, which means `https://`
131|  or `http://localhost`. Over plain HTTP elsewhere, the app falls back to WebGL2.
132|- **No special isolation headers:** PhotoCraft doesn't use `SharedArrayBuffer`, so it doesn't
133|  need `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` or `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy`. If your site already sends
134|  COEP `require-corp`, also send `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin` (or `cross-origin`
135|  when the files live on a CDN) on the app's files.
136|
137|nginx example:
138|
139|```nginx
140|location /photocraft/ {
141|    types { application/wasm wasm; text/javascript js; text/html html; }
142|    gzip on;
143|    gzip_types application/wasm text/javascript text/html;
144|    # The first matching line wins, so the files that keep their names come first.
145|    location ~* (index\.html|app/photocraft-web\.js|app/parts\.txt)$ { add_header Cache-Control "no-cache"; }
146|    location ~* (\.(wasm|js)|\.part-[a-z]+)$ { add_header Cache-Control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable"; }
147|}
148|```

152|## Fonts
153|
154|The app has two fonts of its own, Inter and JetBrains Mono: a browser offers no system fonts, and
155|embedding more would push the wasm over the size gate. A host can serve more fonts next to the
156|app. They show in the font menus straight away, and a family's files are downloaded the first time
157|it is picked or a document's text needs it, so starting the app costs one small text file.
158|
159|1. Put the font files (`.ttf`, `.otf`, `.ttc`) anywhere under `fonts/` next to `index.html`.
160|2. List them in `fonts/manifest.txt`, one file per line, in the format of
161|   [craft-fonts](https://github.com/storytold/craft-fonts)' own `fonts/manifest.txt`:
162|
163|   ```text

165|   Open Sans | Regular | fonts/open-sans/OpenSans[wdth,wght].ttf
166|   Open Sans | Italic | fonts/open-sans/OpenSans-Italic[wdth,wght].ttf
167|   Lobster | Regular | fonts/lobster/Lobster-Regular.ttf | Latn,Cyrl | OFL-1.1 | fonts/lobster/OFL.txt

172|   font menu shows once the file is in. The path is relative to the site root and can't leave it
173|   (no `..`, no `/` at the start, no other host). A variable font is one line: the style menu offers
174|   the weights of its `wght` axis.

178|`fonts/manifest.txt` and the files it lists: `PHOTOCRAFT_WEB_FONTS_DIR=<that folder>
179|packaging/web/package.sh` copies the manifest, the fonts and their licences into the zip, keeping
180|their paths. Without `fonts/manifest.txt` (a 404) nothing changes.

182|Serving: let `fonts/manifest.txt` revalidate (`Cache-Control: no-cache`) so edits show up; cache

188|
189|```html
190|<iframe
191|  src="https://example.com/photocraft/"
192|  title="PhotoCraft image editor"
193|  style="width: 100%; height: 720px; border: 0;"
194|  allow="fullscreen; clipboard-read; clipboard-write"

199|- The app fills the iframe and follows its size, so size the iframe and not the app.

## MCP bridge

`photocraft-automation` provides an MCP server built on the official Rust SDK (`rmcp`). It runs in one of two modes:

- **Headless** (`photocraft-cli mcp`): an in-process `photocraft_engine::Session`. There is no window.
- **Bridge** (`photocraft-cli mcp --bridge 127.0.0.1:7878 --control-token-file <path>`): every tool is forwarded to a running `photocraft --control 7878 --control-token-file <path>` over this protocol, so agents see and drive the live app.

The bridge keeps one authenticated TCP connection open, and drops and reconnects before a call once the connection has been idle long enough that the app (which closes idle connections after 30s) may have dropped it. A transport failure while sending a request or waiting for its reply, including a reply timeout, drops the connection and reports that the operation may have completed; inspect the document before retrying an edit.
